title: Retelling arrival in Chicago and the Hyde Park job
summary: She repeats how she got off the streetcar at the Burlington Building, found Helen Winston and was taken to Hyde Park for a $6-a-week job peeling potatoes.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: But now, I was going to ask you that also. Now, you were very young and you were in Chicago without your family.
You ran away from home. So where did you live? Did you have an apartment?
No. Not here. When I got off -- I told you about my school teacher giving me the pass?
Did I tell you all of that?

Her name was Miss Florida Edgerton. Florida Cummings was her name. I didn't know her name was Edgerton till later years. And I didn't know that the gentleman that was beside her was her husband, you know. But I know that I got on with the lady and the gentleman. The school teacher, my school teacher was the one I was interested in. And I got off the streetcar -- Lord, have mercy. Sometimes I think about that. I got off the streetcar and left them on the streetcar, but when I got off, like I'm -- I was facing this way when I got off, and there was a big building called the Burlington Building. I'll never forget it. And I wandered up some steps, and there was a lady washing, and I asked this lady if she knew a girl by the name of Ellen Winston. See, I had known that there was a girl in Chicago by the name of Ellen Winston. Her mother and my mother were friends. But I didn't know where she lived. But being young and not knowing, I thought if she was in Chicago, anyplace in Chicago would be all right. I could go anyplace in Chicago and people would know where she was. So this lady was washing. I asked her if she knew a girl by the name of Ellen Winston. And she said, 'No, I don't know anybody by the name of Ellen Winston, but there's a girl that lives here by the name of Helen Winston.' She had changed her name, see? To Helen. And she says, 'This

is her Sunday off." And I said, "Well, will you please, ma'am, let me stay here till she comes?" And she said yes. And she said, "Honey, what are you doing here? Where are you from?" And I said, "Well, --" I told her I was from Memphis, you know, and she said, "You are? Does your mother know where you are?" And I said, "No, ma'am." So she said, "Well, you just sit down," and she said, "Are you hungry," you know, and I said, "No, ma'am." I was too glad that that was where Helen lived, you know. So I sat there, and when the girl came it was Helen. This girl that I was looking for. So she said, "Pig, what in the world are you doing here?" Because they called me Pig, you know. And I said, "I ran away from home." So she said, "How did you get here?" And I said, "Well, Miss Florida brought me on a child's pass." She had an eight year old child's pass, you see. So she said, "Well, you sit down there. Wait till I get my shoes off." I don't remember whether her feet were hurting, or whether it was snowing or what, but anyhow, I know she took her shoes off. And so she says, "Well, you just wait a minute." So she took this lady back in the back. I don't know what she said to her, but she must have asked the lady to let me stay there, you know. So evidently the lady said all right. So, but anyhow, when she went to work the next day, she put a dress, a long dress, on me. Because I had on some little red shoes, you know, and a little bitty dress. I wasn't nothing but a kid. And she put a dress a
little longer on me and took me out to Hyde Park where she was working. She was second cook out there, you know.

So she spoke to the lady, and the lady let me work, and she gave me $6.00 a week, room and board. $6.00 a week -- listen -- room and board, and said I could stay there, you know. That's room and board, $6.00 a week. And gave me the job. Peeling potatoes. Wasn't that wonderful?
